# Steering {#sec-steering}

<div data-life="status" data-stage="1.0"></div>

The first animal has no memory, no hunger and no idea of good or bad. It can do one thing: turn what it sees into
movement. This stage evolves a brain that does that, from random wiring, until the animal finds food and eats it.

Everything after this stage is added to this brain.

## The world: berries and onions

The world holds four kinds of berry bush and wild onions. All of it is food and nothing is dangerous. An animal
that stands still starves, and so does one that walks without getting anywhere, because moving costs energy. The
only way to live is to get to a bush that carries berries, bite, and go on to the next one.

The animal eats what it grasps. Picking something up and carrying it comes much later.

<div data-life="settings" data-stage="1.0"></div>

## The biology: steering

The oldest animals with a front and a back were small worms, and what set them apart from jellyfish and sponges
was that they could go somewhere. A body with a front end, sense organs on it, and a clump of neurons behind them
can do something a net of nerves spread through the body cannot: turn towards what is good and away from what is
bad. In *A Brief History of Intelligence* this is the first of the breakthroughs, *steering*.

The circuit for it is small. In the worm *C. elegans*, with 302 neurons, sensory neurons connect to a few layers
of interneurons, and those to the motor neurons, with some sensory neurons wired to motor neurons directly. A
direct connection is a reflex. The interneurons in between let several senses be weighed against each other
before the muscles move.

## The circuit

- A **ganglion** of sixteen excitatory and eight inhibitory interneurons. The eyes connect to it, its neurons
  connect to each other, and it connects to the motor neurons.
- **Reflex arcs**: direct connections from the eyes to the motor neurons.

Every synapse in this brain is evolved: which ones exist, and how strong they are. Nothing is designed and nothing
changes during a life.

The brain sees the outside world only. It does not feel its stomach, and it does not notice whether a bite gave
it anything. Those senses enter the brain in later stages, through cells made for them.

## Watching it work

One animal from the last generation, walking up to a bush and eating. The rows below the picture are the neurons
of the ganglion; there is nothing in them to read, and that is the point. No neuron here stands for anything. The
behaviour is spread over all of them, wherever evolution happened to put it.

## Results

The curve has two parts. The brain first evolves from random wiring in short lives, because at the start nearly
every animal dies young and longer lives would only cost computing time. Then the population is given lives four
times as long, and the curve jumps: the same animals can now collect four times as much well-fed lifetime. In a
short life an animal that ate once and then stood still could reach the end. In a long life it cannot, and over
the generations that follow the standing still is selected away. Every later stage has these long lives.

<div data-life="curves" data-stage="1.0"></div>

<div data-life="summary" data-stage="1.0"></div>

This stage has no control: there is no earlier brain to compare it with. The lesions show the only thing they can
here, that the animal depends on its ganglion. The direct reflex arcs alone are far from enough.

<div data-life="lesions" data-stage="1.0"></div>

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What did not work: all the food at once"}
In earlier runs every bush was full when the animals were born. The animals filled their stomachs within the
first tenth of their life and kept eating, the bushes were stripped by the middle of it, and since a bush takes
long to regrow, most animals then starved together. Whatever an animal might have done better later in life could
not show, and holding back could not pay: whoever waited found nothing left.

Starting most bushes empty, each at a random point of its regrowth, turned that stock into a steady flow. The
share of bushes carrying berries now stays about the same from the first tenth of a life to its end, and so does
the average stomach. The animals still bite when their stomach is full; nothing in this brain can feel the
stomach yet.
:::
